5.text: The Maritime Chukchee and Eskimo have foot-races (Plate XXX, Fig. 1)

6.text: and wrestling-matches (Plate XXXI, Fig. 1) of the same character as those above

7.text: described, as well as nearly all the other sports which we shall now take up.

8.text: I have already noted the fighting-contests of former times and the physical

9.text: exercises with stones (Plate XXVIII, Fig. 1) and trunks of trees.¹ In all exercises

10.text: long and continuous running plays the most important part. The common

11.text: expression for these exercises is “becoming lighter of foot” (inetviˊrkɪn). Even

12.text: at the present time, if a young man is vanquished by an unfriendly rival in

13.text: a wrestling-contest, he will sometimes train for a whole year, dragging heavy

14.text: loads, running, carrying burdens, etc., in order to acquire more agility and

15.text: strength for another contest. Cases of this kind are often mentioned in tales.

16.text: For instance, in the legend of Talo² it is stated that the hero lies idle in his

17.text: tent for about a year, eating an enormous amount and storing up fat and

18.text: muscle. Then suddenly he starts training. At first he is so slow in dragging

19.text: a small sledge behind him, that the moving train of his family gets far ahead

20.text: of him, and he reaches the camping-place only late the next morning. He

21.text: perseveres, however, in his exercises, and from day to day increases his speed

22.text: and the load he is drawing. On the twentieth day he is able to pull six

23.text: loaded sledges, and still keep ahead of the moving train. All this time he

24.text: eats nothing and does not enter his tent, sleeping for only a few hours each

25.text: night out in the open on the snow. After that he practises other exercises.

26.text: For whole days he will throw his lance or jump over the tents, across the

27.text: lakes, or over large forests from one border to the other, until he feels ready

29.text: Tossing in blankets is a kind of religious performance with the Maritime

30.text: Chukchee and Eskimo, and will therefore be described later, in the chapters

31.text: dealing with this subject. Other amusements of less importance are practised

32.text: by grown people and children whenever occasion presents, without prizes being

34.text: Jumping-matches are often arranged on the spur of the moment by young

35.text: people in camps or villages. Each tries to make the longest jump possible,

36.text: keeping his heels together, and getting a start by a few preliminary jumps.

37.text: Arm-pulling, finger-pulling, neck-pulling, and stick-pulling are practised in

38.text: pairs. For these the contestants lock arms or fingers, have a rawhide loop

39.text: passed around their necks, or put their feet sole to sole and grasp the same

42.text: Young women amuse themselves with a game similar to our skip-rope.
